CSCP Learning System 2024 · Module 4 · Section C · Topic 1

Inventory: Forms, Functions, Costs, and Financial Impact

Why organizations hold inventory, what it costs, where to position it, how to manage it in aggregate and item by item, and how finance sees it.

Source: APICS/ASCM CSCP Learning System 2024 (v5.2), Module 4 Scope: Section C, Topic 1: Inventory Format: study summary in original wording

The short version

Five ideas to remember

01

Cost and asset at once. Inventory is a necessary cost of doing business and, managed well, a strategic asset that decouples supply from demand.

02

Type is not function. Type answers "where is it held?"; function answers "why do we hold it?".

03

Costs trade off. Lowering one inventory cost can raise another, so decisions are made on the total.

04

Position and policy. Echelons, planning mode, aggregate and item rules, and ABC classes shape where and how much to hold.

05

Finance sees it differently. Inventory ties up working capital and needs financing, so involve finance before big changes.

40–50%of a supply chain's invested working capital can be tied up in inventory
15–40%typical range of annual carrying cost as a share of inventory value
80/15/5classic split of annual monetary value across ABC classes

1
Inventory road map

What inventory is, and why it matters

Inventory is a major investment for many organizations, so supply chain managers need to understand its forms, functions, and costs, how to position it, how to manage it, and how finance views it.

How finance sees it
ASCM definition (paraphrased)Inventory is the stock or items used to support production (raw materials and work-in-process), supporting activities (maintenance, repair, and operating supplies), and customer service (finished goods and spare parts).

A necessary cost

Organizations carry inventory because it is a cost of doing business. Because it is a cost, they keep searching for the optimum level: the one that maximizes profit, production efficiency, and customer service.

A strategic asset

Managed correctly, inventory is an investment. It can decouple demand and supply, protecting the organization against variability on either side.

Before adding stock: five alternatives

Using inventory to protect against variability costs money and uses space, so management may look for ways to avoid carrying more than desired:

1

Sharper demand signals

Improve demand forecasting and/or use actual demand orders.

2

Steadier supply

Reduce variability in the quality, amount, and timing of supply deliveries.

3

Shorter cycles

Shorten production cycle times.

4

Reliable equipment

Maintain production equipment carefully.

5

Keep it moving

Keep inventory in motion rather than waiting in queues and warehouses.

2
Types of inventory

Five types, defined by where inventory sits

Classification depends on the point of reference: a raw material supplier's finished good becomes the manufacturer's raw material the moment it transfers.

Each type serves particular functions, and all of them add flexibility to the supply chain when they are held at optimum levels. The first three types follow the product through the plant; the last two cut across them.

  • Raw materials, WIP, finished goods: the production sequence.
  • In-transit: some amount of every other type is always on the move.
  • MRO: supports production but never enters the product.

Raw materials

Purchased parts, materials, or subassemblies that have been acquired but have not yet entered production.

Work in process (WIP)

Goods in various stages of completion, from material released for processing to material awaiting final inspection and acceptance. Value has been added but it is not yet finished. It can include held subassemblies for a bill of materials.

Finished goods

Finished, ready-to-use products waiting to be purchased by the customer.

In-transit (distribution)

Material moving between locations that are usually geographically separated, for example finished goods shipped from a plant to a distribution center.

MRO

Spare parts, lubricants, hand tools, and cleaning supplies needed to maintain production but not part of the final product.

Expensed, not an asset

In-transit: the easy-to-miss stock

Counting only what is currently in stock can omit a significant share of total inventory. A typical example is inventory on containerships in international shipments.

It is measured as the average annual inventory in transit, a function of transit time in days and annual demand. Reducing it means finding ways to cut transit time, because less volume needs to be in transit at any moment.

MRO: its own management challenges

MRO supports routine maintenance and emergency repairs. Attention to machinery and MRO forecasting can cut equipment costs and downtime.

  • Often kept in several dispersed locations, so accumulation and use are hard to account for
  • Risks: obsolescence, buying items already in stock, unnoticed pilferage
  • Purchase requisitions are often the only trigger, and their frequency and small size are an administrative burden

Where organizations find improvement

Investing management time in MRO can pay off. The module points to four levers: the size of the MRO investment, the number of suppliers, the controls over MRO, and the ordering process.

  • Corporate credit cards for small-value items
  • A full-service distributor with an online requisition system
  • With enough volume, a distributor employee on site, offering fast replenishment so less needs to be stocked
  • Centralized MRO storage
3
Functions of inventory

Why hold inventory at all?

Inventory can be seen as both an asset and a liability. Its functions answer one question: "Why have inventory in the supply chain?"
FunctionWhat it doesKey points from the module
Cycle stock / lot-size inventoryDepletes gradually as customer orders arrive and is replenished cyclically when supplier orders arriveThe main function of inventory (available-for-sale or sold goods). In aggregate, it may be called pipeline inventory. It is lot-size inventory when bought or made in quantities larger than needed, for quantity or full-truck discounts or to match production batch sizes
Anticipation inventoryExtra stock above basic pipeline stock to cover projected demandCovers rising sales trends, planned promotions, seasonal swings, plant shutdowns, and vacations. It supports the demand plan, including peaks and valleys. Under a level production strategy, it may mean building inventory before it is needed
Buffer inventoryKeeps throughput steady at work centersMaterials awaiting further processing or a work backlog deliberately kept behind a work center. In the theory of constraints, buffers can be time or material. Some organizations adjust buffer sizes dynamically as a lever to protect throughput
Safety stock (fluctuation inventory)Protects against miscalculations of timing or quantityReduces variability in demand and/or supply, supports service targets, and cuts stockout costs. Example: a supplier suddenly goes bankrupt and safety stock keeps production going while a replacement is found
Hedge inventoryManages risk by building, buying, or contractually securing extra stock at a set priceUsed when supply could be threatened or prices could rise. It involves speculating on weather, the economy, strikes, civil strife, or political action. The term is not widely used, but the practice is
Using safety stock: a normal, monitored eventUsing safety stock for unplanned demand is normal to a point. Policy can set an acceptable frequency of use. Use more often than the target is an exception suggesting not enough planned cycle stock. Use less (or never) suggests too much safety stock.
Safety stock vs safety lead timeWhen delivery times fluctuate, safety stock may suit A and B items (fast and medium-fast movers). For C items (slow movers), inventory would grow too much because the stock is rarely needed, so safety lead time should be used instead.

Decoupling: the idea behind buffers and safety stock

ASCM definition (paraphrased)Decoupling creates independence between the supply and use of material. Typically, inventory is allocated between operations so that swings in the supplying operation's rate do not constrain the next operation's rate.

Raw-material example

A stock of raw materials decouples a manufacturer from its suppliers. The sawmill wants a ready supply of trees; the furniture maker wants enough lumber to process. Supply and demand can then run at different, independent rates.

Scheduling example

Many products are made in batches on shared work centers, so some production may happen earlier than needed to avoid bottlenecks. That builds some WIP before it is needed, which is a trade-off to optimize across the whole flow.

Managers look for a cheaper route

Decoupling is often necessary, but supply chain managers look for ways to reach the same goals without the holding costs, by reducing variability in quality, quantity, or delivery time.

4
Inventory costs

Six costs that pull against each other

The costs are interrelated: a decrease in one may cause an increase in another. Inventory managers set order amounts and timing to reduce acquisition, carrying, and ordering costs without sacrificing customer service.

This balancing is needed at every stage: the retailer and distributor order finished goods, the manufacturer orders components and supplies, the supplier orders its own materials, and so on. An order schedule helps coordinate these flows.

1

Acquisition cost

The cost to obtain one or more units: order quantity × unit cost. Also called product cost or purchase price.

2

Landed cost

Product cost plus logistics (warehousing, transportation, handling). Purchased: price paid + transport to site + customs + insurance. Internally sourced: direct labor, direct materials, and factory overhead.

3

Carrying (holding) cost

A percentage of inventory value per unit of time, usually one year. A variable cost that rises with the inventory level. Detailed below.

4

Ordering cost

Costs that rise with the number of orders, not their size: clerical work to prepare, release, monitor, and receive orders; physical handling; inspections; and setup costs.

5

Backorder, lost sale, lost customer

Customer-service costs. A backorder (stockout) is an unfilled order or commitment. Hard to quantify, but can be proxied, for example by the % of orders shipped on schedule.

6

Capacity variance cost

The cost of changing capacity beyond a "normal" range: overtime, extra shifts, layoffs, or plant closings.

Carrying cost in detail

Storage costs

Rent, operating cost, taxes, material handling, equipment leases, depreciation, power. Allocated to SKUs by cube, weight, or density.

Large, dense, or hard-to-handle goods cost more to store.

Capital costs

The return creditors and investors expect because the money could be invested elsewhere (opportunity cost). Financing comes from debt and equity (including retained earnings).

The weighted mix is the WACC, usable as a required return that inventory sales must exceed.

Risk costs

Sensitivity to loss of value: perishability, speed of obsolescence, likelihood of theft. Includes insurance, value reductions, and write-offs.

Risk can be quantified subjectively, as in the example below.

Risk cost, illustrated

The module's example attaches a subjective risk to inventory: a 2% decline in value per day from obsolescence. At that rate, stock held longer than 50 days is considered valueless.

Chart drawn from the example's stated rate (2% × 50 days = 100%). It illustrates the idea; it is not an exhibit from the module.

Ordering, backorder, and capacity variance: where the trade-offs sit

LeverCost that fallsCost that can rise
Order less oftenOrdering cost (fewer orders)Inventory holding cost
Level production through the yearCapacity variance cost (no overtime, layoffs, closings)Inventory holding cost in low-demand periods
Hold more safety stockStockout, lost sale, and lost customer costInventory costs (policy balances the two)

Ways to cut ordering cost

  • Electronic forms and payment transfers
  • Less frequent ordering (at the price of more holding cost)
  • Prepare setups off the work site while machines are still running the prior order, shortening shutdown time

What setup cost includes

Labor to clean machinery and make necessary adjustments or modifications. It requires shutting machines down, which is why reducing shutdown time matters.

5
Inventory planning

Planning mode, location, and level

Inventory planning has two major components: where to locate inventory and the desired level of each item at each chosen location.
ASCM definition (paraphrased)Inventory planning is the activities and techniques of determining desired levels of items (raw materials, WIP, or finished products), including order quantities and safety stock levels. It can be centralized, decentralized, or a hybrid.

Centralized

Inventory is pushed to later stages by the lead organization or channel master. Later stages, such as DCs, have no say in what they receive, though the central system tries to replace what sells and plans for seasonal effects.

Can minimize overall inventory · But may respond slowly to local demand

Decentralized

Each stage determines its own requirements and places orders independently, so there is no coordination expense.

Risk the bullwhip effect, especially if actual customer demand is not visible to all stages

Hybrid

Centralized planning up to a certain point in the chain (for example, the distribution centers), then decentralized planning at all later points.

Centralized and hybrid planning have grown in popularity because decentralized planning can create bullwhip effects.

Where should inventory be located?

Inventory belongs wherever in the distribution network it can serve a valid purpose: as a buffer between stages, to reduce overall cost, and to meet customer service goals. It can sit in warehouses, in retail locations, or in transit.

ASCM definitions (paraphrased)Warehouse: a place to receive, store, and ship materials. Decisions cover site selection, number of facilities, layout, and methods of receiving, storing, and retrieving.
Distribution center (DC): typically a finished-goods warehouse built for rapid, demand-driven distribution to retailers, wholesalers, or directly to customers. Cross-docking warehouses are another type.

Echelons: a level of supply chain nodes

Treating each stage of inventory handling as an echelon is a good way to reason about locations. Each echelon adds operating expense, holds inventory, adds to cycle time, and expects to make a profit.

Choosing the number of echelons

  • Organizations decide how many echelons to have; each one adds material, labor, overhead, and inventory cost.
  • Consolidation warehouses could be omitted entirely.
  • A direct-to-customer model has no wholesalers or retailers.
  • Strategic network design sets the optimum number, then analysis sets the number and geographic location of sites, using network modeling, operations research, and decision support systems to find the lowest total cost of ownership of storage, handling, and transportation for a chosen service level.

Echelon inventory policy

Inventory at a given point is defined to include all inventory at that echelon and at every later point, including all in-transit stock after it.

Benefit: demand from all lower points is aggregated, giving more accurate order quantities and levels. The process repeats, in more detail, at each lower echelon. Hybrid systems can use it up to where centralized planning ends and rely on visibility after that.

What each echelon contributes

NodeBenefit it can provide
Suppliers' warehousesA buffer against manufacturing orders
Consolidation warehousesLower transportation cost by grouping shipments from several sources into fewer shipments to a manufacturer or assembler
Manufacturing warehousesA buffer for the process (raw materials and WIP) and for later echelons (finished goods), i.e., decoupling between nodes
Distribution centersA buffer for later echelons; as break-bulk sites they receive large shipments (economies of scale) and ship individual orders; they can also consolidate shipments from many vendors
WholesalersMay buffer, consolidate, or break bulk
RetailersImmediate access to inventory, and possibly other services

Consolidation and break-bulk

Cut transport cost and can reduce inventory, especially slow movers, which can ship in smaller quantities when combined with other stock.

Sorting

Cross-docking, assembly, and mixing.

Seasonal storage

Produce year-round, sell in one season.

Reverse logistics

Sites for returns, remanufacturing, repair, remarketing, and disposal or recycling.

Levels of inventory

The ideal vs the realIn an ideal network, materials and components are never at rest in a warehouse: they move until they arrive just in time at each location. That state is hard or impossible to reach because demand fluctuates from the ultimate customer backward, and accidents and bad weather intervene. The manager's challenge is to assess future demand as accurately as possible and keep inventory as low as possible without disrupting delivery. This relies on demand management and forecasting, distribution requirements planning, warehouse management systems, and transportation management systems.
6
Inventory management

Policy, aggregate view, and item view

Inventory management is the branch of business management concerned with planning and controlling inventories. It is needed wherever inventory is carried, and it is viewed from two angles.

Supply chain perspective

Concerned with inflows and outflows at each stage, from ordering raw materials to handing finished goods to the customer. It benefits strongly from inventory visibility (the extent to which inventory information is shared within a firm and with partners) and from supply chain collaboration.

Enterprise (internal process) perspective

Inventory feeds into production and results from it, so planners, master planners, and production schedulers coordinate with each other at each level of production planning.

Competing interests

FunctionWhat it wants from inventory management (Exhibit 4-25)
Purchasing and materials managementAdequate raw materials at low inventory cost
Manufacturing and financeEfficient, low-cost production balanced against low inventory cost
Sales and marketingEnough inventory to meet customer delivery requests and service levels

Inventory is managed both as an overall strategic concern (aggregate) and at the individual item level. Each method is necessary, and together they cover strategic and operational needs.

Inventory policy

Inventory policy formalizes strategic inventory decisions so they are implemented consistently. It can be broad (centralized or decentralized planning and warehousing, communication and coordination frequency, a geographic positioning strategy such as postponement) or specific (rules for order quantities and timing, when to act on exceptions, how much of an item to buy versus make).

Organizations weigh six factors when setting it:

Customer demand

Known in advance or forecast; policy must compensate for forecast variability.

Planning horizon

Its length affects needed levels; long-term plans may leave time to change system capacity.

Replenishment lead time

A key input, especially when lead times are long or highly variable.

Product variety

Similar products compete for budget and shelf space, so policies interlock. Families are planned together. Too much variety means too many SKUs and much higher holding cost for make-to-stock products.

Inventory costs

Order costs (production and transportation) and carrying costs.

Customer service requirements

Sets safety stock per item and location, balancing failures to fill orders in acceptable time against rising inventory cost.

Aggregate vs item inventory management

Aggregate level (strategic)

Focus: the financial impact of inventories, aiming for the level that produces the greatest overall profit for the organization and supply chain.

Why aggregate? Analyzing a large number of items one by one is impractical, and aggregate forecasts are more accurate than item-level forecasts because aggregation reduces variability. Aggregate only as far as the groups still give effective analysis.

Used to:

  • Decide which types of inventory to hold
  • Optimize inventory flow and set buffers between stages
  • Match supply with demand
  • Set inventory objectives and policy
  • Calculate inventory costs by category
  • Support S&OP (including production planning), demand management, and resource planning

Item level (operational)

Focus: short-term operational decisions using rules set in inventory policy and/or IT systems.

Rules specify:

  • When to order
  • How to determine order size
  • The relative importance of each item
  • Control procedures for individual items

Goal: translate strategic inventory goals into measurable results: proper production and distribution of each product or SKU.

Link to planning: S&OP plans production at the family (aggregate) level; master scheduling plans it at the item level. Retail locations also need both views. Item management is implemented through inventory planning, inventory models, and inventory control.

Ways to aggregate inventory

Demand pattern

Women's vs men's running shoes

Production process

Both shoe lines made on the same line

Stage of production flow

Raw materials, finished goods

Product or SKU family

Similar functions, different models, packaging, colors, or styles

Distribution pattern

Same source and/or same delivery location or customer zone

Relative value

ABC classification, covered next

ABC inventory classification

ASCM definition (paraphrased)Rank items by decreasing annual dollar volume (price × projected volume) or other criteria, then split the ranking into classes A, B, and C. The principle: effort and money can be saved by applying looser controls to low-dollar-volume items. It applies to inventories, purchasing, and sales, and is often based on the monetary value of inventory at standard cost.
ClassShare of itemsShare of value
Aabout 10–20%about 50–70%
Babout 20%about 20%
Cabout 50%about 10–30%

ASCM Dictionary ranges, as cited in the module.

Pareto at work

ABC applies the Pareto principle: a small share of the population (about 20%) drives a large share of the impact (about 80%). It is a general rule, but often meaningful enough to use. The classic form puts 80% of value in 20% of part numbers (A), 15% in 30% (B), and 5% in 50% (C).

Beyond annual dollarsAnnual monetary volume is only one criterion. Class A items may be high-margin goods, or lower-margin goods with high turnover. Quality concerns or planned upgrades may also shift classes. Some firms refine the scheme: one organization found 1% of its items made up 50% of annual monetary volume, so it added a fourth class and called its system ABCD.

What ABC can be used to drive

1

More effort and money on relationships with A-item suppliers, and none on C-item suppliers

2

Secure storage and extra care in transport for A items, plus quick access to fast-turnover goods

3

More rigorous demand forecasts for A items

4

Prioritizing cycle counting. ERP systems usually keep a separate ABC field for counting, so using ABC as inventory policy may need a different data field

Other aggregate classification methods exist, based on criteria such as individual cost or utility value.

7
Effects of inventory on financial statements

How finance sees inventory

Beyond the things a company owns for sale or production, inventory is all the money currently tied up in the supply chain: as much as 40 to 50 percent of invested working capital.

Inventory can be seen as the buffer that hides flaws in the supply chain, and also as the lubricant that keeps it flexible. A flexible chain responds quickly to internal and external changes such as demand swings, so inventory management strongly affects cash flows and financial position.

The supply chain professional's goal: manage inventory level and cost efficiently while maintaining and improving customer satisfaction.

Too much

Fast delivery and strong satisfaction, but cash tied up in inventory can lead to financial failure.

Too little

Costs cut to nearly nothing, but the company may be unable to deliver, and customers go elsewhere.

The balancing actKeep inventory moving and cash turning over: a relatively high inventory turnover ratio (times per year that cash invested in inventory returns as revenue) and a relatively short cash-to-cash cycle time (which includes the effects of accounts payable and receivable). Financial discussions about inventory are usually framed as reducing inventory, reducing inventory costs, or raising turnover or cash-to-cash speed.

Balance sheet

The balance sheet (statement of financial position) has two sections that must balance under the accounting equation. Inventory is a current asset. In internal management reports it may be split into raw materials, WIP, and finished goods; externally available balance sheets typically show total inventory only.

Raw materials, WIP, finished goods

Current assets→ sold →COGS expense

They do not touch the income statement until the inventory is sold, reduced to fair market value, or written off as obsolete.

MRO inventory

Period expense→Expensed when purchased

It is expensed on the income statement in the period it is bought, not carried as an asset.

An asset also needs financing

To finance assets, more liabilities are needed. Some current assets are also less liquid than others (liquidity is how quickly they convert to cash).

The optimum holding equals projected sales in the demand plan plus an optimal safety stock. Stock expected to sell soon is more liquid; stock beyond the demand plan is less liquid.

Average inventory (quick estimate)

Software can compute it at any time. For a quick estimate, add the inventory value at the start of the period to the value at the end and divide by two.

It is used in performance measures and in inventory space calculations. The module's worked example (Exhibit 4-28) is an image, so no figures are reproduced here.

Risks of carrying too much inventory

Embedded cost

Balance-sheet value includes production cost. On sale, direct materials, direct labor, and factory overhead become an expense offsetting revenue and reducing cash, so only the margin contributes to net income.

Magnified quality issues

If a defect is found, more stock with the same defect multiplies scrap, repair, or replacement cost.

Obsolescence and spoilage

The longer stock sits on the books, the likelier it is written down to fair market value or written off entirely.

Write-off consequences

Physical removal, and an expense for materials, labor, and overhead with no offsetting revenue. Strict accounting rules apply. Accountants often create an inventory reserve in anticipation.

Valuation on the books

Financial accounting methods

Valuation follows specific rules based on the age distribution of inventory. Methods can leave the accounting value closer to or further from market value:

FIFOLIFOWeighted average costSpecific identification

For managerial accounting, inventory can be valued at standard cost; variances from actual cost are adjusted at period end and show up in the financial statements.

The reported figure may also include inventory that is reserved, obsolete, damaged, or otherwise unsalable, some of which will later be written off.

Practical ruleChanges to inventory levels change accounting values and the financing needed. Supply chain managers should consult financial managers with enough advance notice to change levels while keeping the organization solvent and in good standing with creditors and investors.

Income statement and cash flow

Income statement

Gross profit = revenue − COGS. COGS covers the direct labor, direct materials, and factory overhead of goods sold in the year, so reducing those elements raises gross profit directly.

Cutting costs lifts profit faster than raising sales volume, because variable costs rise with revenue. Lowering variable supply chain costs raises the margin on inventory without raising prices.

Caution on building ahead: producing inventory early can defer COGS until it sells, but operating (period) expenses are expensed as incurred, which can strain financial ratios, and cash goes out during the build-up. Finance needs to plan for it.

Statement of cash flows

A company does not want all of its capital tied up in inventory. Insufficient cash means expensive borrowing, or quick failure if funds cannot be raised.

Net increase in inventory → cash fallsNet decrease in inventory → cash rises

Inventory changes can also affect loan covenants: lender requirements to maintain certain financial ratios. Even a reduction can cause one-time adjustments that affect reporting, though the long-term effect of reducing inventory is usually positive.

Case: when a good idea breaches a covenant

A supply chain manager finds slow-selling stock and proposes cutting inventory by €60 million. The CFO raises a concern: the bank's loan covenant requires owners' equity to be twice liabilities (2:1).

−€60m

Inventory cut. Best case, cash rises by a few million euros; worst case, the company pays to scrap the stock.

−€60m

Equity falls. Assuming no net change in income, retained earnings drop by the same amount to keep the balance sheet in balance.

−€30m

Liabilities must fall by half as much to hold the 2:1 ratio, a large burden on cash flow.

Default

If the covenant fails, the company is in technical default and its debts could become due immediately, so the change cannot be made right away.

Lessons from the case(1) Consult finance before proposing a major inventory change, so finance can find a way to accommodate it while keeping the company solvent. (2) Create financial reservations for obsolete stock, so finance can prepare for write-offs.

Key terms

Terms at a glance

TermPlain-language meaning
Cycle stock / pipeline inventoryStock that depletes with orders and is replenished cyclically; pipeline inventory in aggregate
Lot-size inventoryCycle stock bought or made in larger quantities than needed, for discounts or batch sizes
Anticipation inventoryExtra stock to cover planned peaks, promotions, seasons, and shutdowns
Buffer inventoryMaterial or time kept in front of a work center to protect throughput
Safety stockStock held against errors in timing or quantity of demand and supply
Hedge inventoryExtra stock secured at a set price against supply threats or price rises
DecouplingMaking supply and use independent so one operation's swings do not constrain the next
Acquisition costOrder quantity × unit cost
Landed costProduct cost plus logistics (and, for purchases, transport, customs, insurance)
Carrying (holding) costPercentage of inventory value per year: storage, capital, and risk
Ordering costCost that rises with the number of orders, including setup
Backorder (stockout)An unfilled customer order or commitment
EchelonA level of supply chain nodes, each adding expense, inventory, cycle time, and an expected profit
Inventory visibilityHow far inventory information is shared inside a firm and with partners
ABC classificationRanking items by annual dollar volume and grouping them into A, B, and C classes
Inventory reserveAn accounting account that lowers inventory value in anticipation of write-offs
9
For discussion

Six reflection questions for your organization

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

Drawn from Topic 1 as material for team discussion. Answers depend on each organization's situation and should be backed by facts rather than perception.

  1. Counting everything. Does your view of total inventory include in-transit stock and the way MRO is treated (expensed, dispersed, ordered by small requisitions)?
  2. Type vs function. For your largest stock positions, which function does each one serve (cycle, anticipation, buffer, safety, hedge)? Is any stock held without a clear purpose?
  3. Trade-offs. When someone proposes reducing one inventory cost (fewer orders, level production, less safety stock), which other cost would rise, and who bears it?
  4. Position and policy. How many echelons does your chain have, is planning centralized, decentralized, or hybrid, and is actual customer demand visible to every stage?
  5. Aggregate and item. Are your ABC classes still defensible (value only, or margin, turnover, quality, and upcoming changes too), and are controls tighter where value is concentrated?
  6. Finance first. Before the next significant stock reduction or build-up, has finance reviewed the effect on covenants, cash flow, reserves, and write-offs?
